title: Minimum Valuation and Assessment Framework
summary: This thread covers the mechanism of setting 'Minimum Value' or 'Tariff Value' for specific goods to prevent under-invoicing, and the broader assessment framework. It has evolved from general valuation principles to specific minimum value mandates for high-value goods like motor vehicles, sugar, and meat.

evolution.valuation_method: Shifted from general international market price assessment to specific minimum value mandates.
evolution.enforcement: Strengthened by explicitly defining minimum value as the assessable value.

timeline.change: Established foundational legal basis for valuation based on competitive international trade prices.
Initial establishment of minimum value for motor vehicles.
Expansion to tariff values for various goods.
Introduced specific minimum value thresholds for used/reconditioned motor vehicles.
Updated minimum value determinations for new motor vehicles.
Formalization of minimum value as the mandatory dutiable value.
Application of minimum value to meat products.
Amended assessment scope to clarify total duty subject to specific provisions.

Customs Act 1969: The Government is empowered by section 25(3) of this Act to set minimum valuation criteria for specific imported goods.
First Schedule: This instrument establishes minimum valuation conditions for new motor vehicles and automobiles classified under specific headings of this schedule.
Customs Duty: The collection of this duty on new motor vehicles and automobiles is subject to the minimum valuation requirements established by this order.
Manufacturer’s Price Certificate: Importers are required to submit a valid price certificate from the vehicle manufacturer to determine the minimum value for customs purposes.

In cases where the manufacturer's certificate is unavailable, a certificate from a marketing company with at least thirty percent ownership by the manufacturer may be accepted upon submission of proof of such ownership to the Customs Commissioner.
Certificates issued by agents or dealers appointed by the manufacturer are explicitly excluded from being accepted for valuation purposes.

The value derived from this certificate serves as the minimum threshold for customs valuation, unless the declared transaction value of the vehicle is higher, in which case the higher declared value prevails.

Manufacturer’s Price Certificate: Importers must submit a manufacturer's invoice for the valuation of imported vehicles.
In cases where the importer is not the manufacturer, the invoice issued by the exporter must be certified by the manufacturer.
If a manufacturer directly issues invoices, invoices from third-party exporters will not be accepted for customs valuation purposes.

The manufacturer-certified invoice serves as the minimum value for assessment, though higher values found in recognized international publications or official price lists must be used if they exceed the invoice price.
The valuation of new vehicles must not be lower than the value of used, old, or reconditioned vehicles of the same brand, model, and cylinder capacity from the same country of origin.
